title: Why you hear an echo in a canyon but not in a small room
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: Why do I hear echoes in mountains but not at home?
How far away does a wall need to be for an echo?

explain.say: When you shout in a canyon, your voice spreads out at about 343 metres per second. When it hits a big hard cliff, much of it bounces back like a ball off a wall.

explain.say: That reflected sound travels all the way back to you. If it arrives a tenth of a second or more after you shouted, your brain hears it as a separate copy: an echo.

explain.say: In a small room the walls are only a few metres away, so reflections return almost at once and blend with your voice. That makes the room sound boomy, called reverberation, rather than giving a clear echo.

faq.a: An echo is sound that has bounced off a large hard surface, like a cliff or building, and come back to you late enough to be heard as a separate sound.

faq.q: Why don't I hear an echo in a small room?
faq.a: The walls are so close that the reflected sound returns in less than a tenth of a second. Your brain blends it with the original, so you hear a fuller, boomier sound instead of an echo.
asks: Why are there no echoes at home?

faq.q: How far away does a wall need to be for an echo?
faq.a: At least about 17 metres. The sound must travel there and back, about 34 metres, which takes around a tenth of a second, the shortest gap your ears can separate.
asks: What is the minimum distance for an echo?
How close can a wall be for an echo?

faq.q: Why do soft things stop echoes?
faq.a: Soft, rough or fluffy surfaces like curtains, carpets, snow and trees soak up sound instead of reflecting it. That is why an empty room echoes more than a furnished one.
asks: Why does an empty room echo?

faq.q: Can echoes tell you how far away something is?
faq.a: Yes. Time the echo, multiply by the speed of sound and halve it, because the sound went there and back. Bats, dolphins and ships' sonar all use this trick.
asks: How do you measure distance with an echo?

facts: To hear a separate echo, the reflecting surface must usually be at least about 17 metres away.
Hard, smooth surfaces reflect sound well, while soft, porous ones absorb it.

quiz.say: You shout towards a cliff 170 metres away. About how long until you hear the echo?
quiz.show: Echo from a cliff 170 m away arrives after about…
quiz.why: The sound goes there and back, 340 metres, and sound travels about 343 metres a second, so about 1 second.

wrong.0: Half a second only covers the trip to the cliff, not the way back.
wrong.2: In 5 seconds sound travels over 1.7 kilometres.
